own_scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa
own_scenes.desc: La Costa Oeste fue desde el principio terreno de rap funk: Uncle Jamm’s Army de Rodger Clayton y Egyptian Lover, con disfraces a lo P-Funk y electro-funk desde 1981; Too Short en Oakland, pionero del rap X y de la fusión con bajo real («I Wanna Be Free», con Shorty B). Pero el sonido que arrasó vino del sur de Los Ángeles: N.W.A. (Ice Cube, Dr. Dre, Eazy-E, Yella) y «Straight Outta Compton» (1989), misoginia y rabia, fantasías de agresión contra un sistema que no cede («Fuck tha Police»). Con la apatía de Bush, el crack y las armas, el encarcelamiento de James Brown y la humillación de los ídolos, Ice Cube predijo en Death Certificate (1991) la revuelta de Rodney King de 1992; el hip hop estaba mejor informado que la prensa. Cuando los pleitos encarecieron los samples, Dr. Dre y Snoop volvieron a tocar con músicos: The Chronic (1993). En 1995 el funk estaba en todos los títulos: The G Funk Era de Warren G, Funkdafied de Da Brat, Guerrilla Funk de Paris. «El hip hop salvó el funk», dijo Clinton; ahora le toca al funk salvar al hip hop.

refs.q: The West Coast has been a hotbed of outright funk-oriented rap music from the earliest days of Hip Hop.
refs.para: The West Coast has been a hotbed of outright funk-oriented rap music from the earliest days of Hip Hop. The Los Angeles—based deejay and dance music troupe, Uncle Jamm’s Army, led by Rodger Clayton (Uncle Jamm) and his deejay, known as The Egyptian Lover, had been tearing up Los Angeles—area dance clubs since 1981—wearing fatigues and wild Egyptian tribal-space costumes in the vein of George Clinton’s P-Funk (using Clinton’s “Uncle Jam” concept). By 1984, they were generating a relentless string of Electro-Funk twelve-inch dance singles that challenged Afrika Bambaataa’s domination of the early scene.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

refs.q: This was music for people who don’t give a fuck—or at least people who want to feel like they don’t.
refs.para: This was music for people who don’t give a fuck—or at least people who want to feel like they don’t. The tracks smoked, as then-unknown rappers Ice Cube, Dr. Dre, Eazy E, and Yella turned the very purpose of rap music on its head. Other songs like “Fuck tha Police” and “Gangsta Gangsta” revealed the unbridled contempt for the police force and mainstream society in general that the group had experienced in some form or another. Ultimately, their lyrics amounted to fantasies of aggression against a system that gives no ground. Yet taken out of context, they stand out as pathological adolescent ramblings of unbridled rage. Clearly, however, the crew knew that they were in a position to deliver a load of sex and violence that Americans feared in real life but came to desire in rap music.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

refs.q: Any way you look at it, Hip Hop and funk are inseparable.
refs.para: The Funk is now the central focus in higher forms of Hip Hop. The ideals, the attitudes, and many of the riffs in hard-core Hip Hop owe their existence to the original funk masters, who paved the way by working for creative independence and delivering the truth to their people as they saw fit. Any way you look at it, Hip Hop and funk are inseparable. As George Clinton put it in 1990, “Hip Hop saved The Funk” by bringing it out of the past and into the present. Now it’s time for The Funk to save Hip Hop.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

similar_scenes.name: G-funk: The Chronic, Death Row y Snoop Doggy Dogg
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: Hay un antes y un después de The Chronic (diciembre de 1992): samples de Parliament-Funkadelic, bajos lentos de Moog y músicos tocando encima, un sonido perezoso y amenazante a la vez, con Snoop Doggy Dogg, Nate Dogg, Daz, Warren G, Kurupt, The Lady of Rage y RBX. Lo publicó Death Row, fundada por Dr. Dre, The D.O.C., Dick Griffey y Marion «Suge» Knight, exguardaespaldas que «liberó» a Dre, D.O.C. y Michel’le de Ruthless con el dinero de un traficante preso, Michael «Harry-O» Harris; Interscope (Jimmy Iovine y Ted Field) lo financió y distribuyó. Snoop, de Long Beach, había hecho maquetas con Sir Jinx y formado 213 con Warren G y Nate Dogg; debutó en «Deep Cover». «Nuthin’ but a ‘G’ Thang» se grabó tres veces y vendió ocho millones (siete y medio a chavales blancos): con versiones de radio sin tacos, el gangsta llegó a todas partes, y SoundScan (1991), que contaba ventas reales, demostró su peso. Doggystyle (1993), con «Who Am I (What’s My Name)?» sobre «Atomic Dog», vendió ochocientos mil discos en una semana. Cold 187um (hijo y sobrino de los Hutch de Motown) reclama la invención del G-funk con Above the Law en Black Mafia Life; Warren G, fichado por Def Jam tras «Indo Smoke», lo llevó al pop con «Regulate» (sobre Michael McDonald). Death Row dominó con Dre, Snoop y Tupac y se hundió tras la muerte de este; Knight cumple veintiocho años de cárcel por atropellar mortalmente a Terry Carter en 2015.

podcast.title: Influence on Chop 'N' Screw
podcast.body: G-Funk was the base music that DJ Escriu slowed down and transformed in his Chop 'N' Screw experiments in early 90s Houston, turning it into a "dragged-out" experience. "rellenizaba al gijob hasta convertirlo en una experiencia de ensayarrestrada."

podcast.title: Influence on Early Phonk
podcast.body: Space Goshpar's initial vision for authentic Miami funk was influenced by West Coast G-Funk, integrating its sound into a modern, digital sensibility. "Influenciado por el G-Funk de la costa hueste, Space Goshpar llamó a esta música auténtico funk de Miami y en 2011 lanzó el tema Filda Funk 1990."
